title: Getting Projects Under Control
coreMove: Shift a stuck project from vague worry into forward motion by stating the successful outcome, brain-dumping every moving part, and pulling one next physical action from that inventory.

exampleSpecs.domain: a freelance graphic designer's stalled client rebrand that has sat untouched on her project list for two weeks
exampleSpecs.audience: an independent creative professional juggling four concurrent client accounts
exampleSpecs.stakes: the client is growing impatient and a competing agency is waiting in the wings
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sees that 'do rebrand' was never a project—it was an anxiety—and that a fifteen-minute brain-dump turns the dread-item into seven distinct pieces she can actually schedule

exampleSpecs.domain: a middle school science teacher planning the annual spring science fair while managing three daily preps
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher who carries sole project ownership with no prep period to spare
exampleSpecs.stakes: a custodial booking for the gym will lapse by Friday unless someone confirms it, and no one knows who that someone is
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she catches herself staring at the words 'science fair' on her project list and realizes those two words have done none of the work—she still cannot say what a successful fair looks like or who owns the venue confirmation

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional sales manager whose 'fix the quarterly reporting process' project has been deferred three consecutive cycles
exampleSpecs.audience: a mid-level manager whose discretionary projects are routinely displaced by reactive work
exampleSpecs.stakes: the broken process costs his team four hours every quarter and he is starting to lose credibility with his director
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he is asked to write a handoff memo as if someone else will finish this project—and discovers he cannot write it because he has never defined what 'fixed' looks like in a single sentence

exampleSpecs.domain: a residential contractor managing a kitchen remodel where the homeowners keep adding scope mid-build
exampleSpecs.audience: a small-business owner whose project tracking lives in a construction notebook that has become illegible
exampleSpecs.stakes: margin erosion and a homeowner relationship that turns adversarial when expectations keep slipping
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he stands in the half-demolished kitchen, notebook open, and feels the familiar fog—not because the work is unclear, but because nowhere on any page does it say what a completed kitchen actually means to this client or to him

exampleSpecs.domain: a first-year medical resident coordinating her first research presentation while covering 60-hour clinical weeks
exampleSpecs.audience: an early-career professional for whom discretionary time arrives in 20-minute blocks between patient rounds
exampleSpecs.stakes: missing the conference submission deadline forfeits a fellowship application requirement she cannot recover this year
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: her attending asks what the hold-up is and she hears herself say 'I just haven't had time'—and realizes mid-sentence that she has opened the draft folder six times but never written down what the presentation needs to accomplish or what the single next action is

exampleSpecs.domain: a community theater director whose spring production nearly lost its venue because no one held the booking deadline
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer leader managing a cast and crew with no formal project management background
exampleSpecs.stakes: losing the venue would cancel the production, disappoint a cast of twenty, and sever the company's relationship with the venue owner
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the debrief surfaces that every cast member assumed someone else was tracking the venue—the project existed as a single line item on a shared doc but was never decomposed into owned outcomes with next actions attached to real names
